body:
Andhra Pradesh

The traditional dances of Andhra Pradesh include agricultural, devotional and tribal forms.

DanceAssociationIdentifying feature
DhimsaTribal communities of the Araku Valley and surrounding hillsCoordinated group dancing
Butta BommaluFestive folk traditionLarge decorative figure costumes
VeeranatyamWorship of ShivaVigorous devotional tradition
KolatamCommunity celebrationsRhythmic use of sticks
DappuFolk festivals and processionsDappu percussion instrument
Tappeta GulluNorthern coastal Andhra PradeshTraditional drum-based group performance

Dhimsa, also spelt Dhemsa, is particularly associated with tribal communities in the Eastern Ghats. It is commonly performed by women in groups, accompanied by locally used drums and wind instruments such as the mori.

The Andhra Pradesh tradition of Kolatam has parallels with stick dances in neighbouring states and Gujarat.

Telangana

Gussadi

Gussadi is a tribal dance particularly associated with the Gond communities of the Adilabad region. It is performed during the Dandari celebrations around Deepavali.

Distinctive peacock-feather headgear, traditional costumes and drum accompaniment are major identifying features.

Perini Shivatandavam

Perini Shivatandavam is a traditional martial and devotional dance associated with the Kakatiya period and the worship of Shiva. It is historically associated with male performers and warrior traditions.

Telangana also has the Lambadi dance of the Banjara community, which is associated with colourful costumes, embroidery and community celebrations.

Karnataka

DanceAssociationIdentifying feature
Dollu KunithaKuruba community and Beeralingeshwara worshipLarge dollu drums
VeeragaseShaiva religious traditionVigorous devotional performance
KamsaleMale Mahadeshwara devotional traditionMetal percussion instruments
YakshaganaCoastal KarnatakaFolk dance-drama with elaborate costumes

Dollu Kunitha is distinguished by the use of large drums carried by the performers. Yakshagana, however, is a broader theatrical tradition combining dance, music, acting and storytelling. Instruments associated with Yakshagana include the chande and maddale.

Tamil Nadu

DanceAssociationIdentifying feature
KaragattamRain and fertility-related worship, including MariammanDecorated pot balanced on the head
KummiWomen's festive gatheringsRhythmic clapping
KolattamCommunity and religious celebrationsWooden sticks
Kavadi AttamWorship of MuruganDecorated kavadi carried by devotees
OyilattamRegional folk celebrationsCoordinated group dance
Poikkal Kuthirai AttamFestive folk performanceDummy horse costume

Karagattam may be devotional or performed for entertainment. Traditional accompaniment often includes the nadaswaram and tavil.

Kummi relies prominently on rhythmic clapping, while Kolattam is identified through the use of sticks.

Kerala

Theyyam

Theyyam is a ritual performance associated with North Malabar, particularly Kannur and Kasaragod. It combines dance, worship, music, dramatic representation, elaborate costumes and distinctive facial decoration.

The performance takes place in religious and community settings, including local shrines. Its identifying features include elaborate headgear and percussion accompaniment.

Other traditional forms

FormPrincipal association
Thiruvathirakali or KaikottikaliWomen's circular dance associated with Thiruvathira and festive occasions
OppanaMappila Muslim marriage celebrations
MargamkaliSyrian Christian community tradition
PulikaliOnam celebrations and tiger-themed costumes
MudiyettuRitual theatre and dance-drama based on the conflict between Kali and Darika

Mudiyettu was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010. Kathakali and Mohiniyattam, by contrast, are classical dance traditions associated with Kerala.

Prelims focus

  • Dhimsa: tribal communities of the Araku Valley and adjoining areas.
  • Gussadi: Gond communities of Telangana.
  • Dollu Kunitha: Karnataka, Kuruba community and large drums.
  • Karagattam: Tamil Nadu and balancing a decorated pot.
  • Theyyam: North Malabar, Kerala.
  • Trap: Yakshagana and Mudiyettu are composite theatrical and dance traditions, not simply individual folk dances.

[References: South Central Zone Cultural Centre, Andhra Pradesh dance traditions; Alluri Sitharama Raju district cultural information on Dhimsa; Telangana Tourism, Heritage and Culture and History; Karnataka Tourism, Dollu Kunitha; Kerala Tourism, Theyyam and traditional art forms; Thanjavur tourism cultural information, Folk Arts; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, p. 113; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India; UNESCO, Mudiyettu, Ritual Theatre and Dance Drama of Kerala. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Folk and Tribal Dances of Southern India

body:
Assam

Bihu

Bihu is both the name of a major Assamese festival tradition and a distinctive folk dance. The dance is most closely associated with Rongali Bihu, also called Bohag Bihu, which marks the Assamese New Year and the arrival of spring in April.

Bihu reflects agricultural life, seasonal renewal and social celebration. Young men and women traditionally participate in energetic group performances.

Important musical instruments associated with Bihu include:

  • Dhol: a traditional drum providing rhythm.
  • Pepa: a wind instrument traditionally made using a buffalo horn.
  • Gogona: a vibrating bamboo instrument resembling a jaw harp.
  • Toka: a bamboo clapper.
  • Taal: metallic cymbals.

The 3 principal Bihu festivals are Rongali or Bohag Bihu, Kongali or Kati Bihu, and Bhogali or Magh Bihu. Although all belong to the Assamese agricultural calendar, the lively Bihu dance is especially associated with Rongali Bihu.

Bagurumba

Bagurumba is a traditional dance of the Bodo community. It is particularly associated with celebrations such as Bwisagu, the Bodo spring festival.

Its gentle movements are often compared with the movements of butterflies and birds. Musical accompaniment may include the kham drum, siphung flute and serja string instrument.

Other Assamese folk and tribal traditions include Jhumur, associated with tea-garden communities, and Gumrag, associated with the Mising community and its agricultural celebrations.

Meghalaya

Dance or festival traditionCommunityAssociation
WangalaGaroPost-harvest thanksgiving
Nongkrem danceKhasiReligious thanksgiving and prosperity
Shad Suk MynsiemKhasiSpring thanksgiving celebration
Kashad MastiehKhasi traditionTraditional martial dance

Wangala is associated with thanksgiving to Misi Saljong, a deity connected with agricultural prosperity. Drums are central to the celebration, which is popularly associated with the Hundred Drums Festival.

Nongkrem is particularly associated with the Khasi religious celebration at Smit. Traditional drums and wind instruments accompany the festivities.

Mizoram

Cheraw

Cheraw is the famous bamboo dance of Mizoram. Long bamboo poles are rhythmically opened and closed by seated participants, while other dancers move between them.

The striking of the bamboo poles provides a distinctive rhythmic sound. The dance is an important feature of Mizo cultural celebrations.

Other Mizo dances

Khuallam is traditionally known as a dance of guests and is accompanied by instruments such as gongs and drums.

Chheih Lam is a community dance associated with social gatherings. Rhythmic clapping, drums and bamboo instruments may accompany its songs.

Tripura

Hojagiri

Hojagiri is a distinctive dance of the Reang community, also known as Bru. It is traditionally performed by women and is associated with religious and festive celebrations.

Balance is its most recognisable feature. Performers use objects such as pitchers, bottles and lamps. Traditional musical accompaniment includes the khamb drum, bamboo flute and cymbals.

Garia dance

Garia dance is associated with the worship of Garia and agricultural celebrations among the Tripuri and related communities. The festival expresses hopes for a successful agricultural season, prosperity and collective well-being.

Mamita is another dance and festive tradition associated with agricultural life in Tripura.

Prelims focus

  • Bihu: Assam, Rongali Bihu and buffalo-horn pepa.
  • Bagurumba: Bodo community of Assam.
  • Wangala: Garo community of Meghalaya.
  • Cheraw: bamboo dance of Mizoram.
  • Hojagiri: Reang or Bru community of Tripura.
  • Trap: Bagurumba belongs to Assam, whereas Wangala belongs primarily to the Garo tradition of Meghalaya.

[References: Incredible India, Bihu Dance and Arts and Crafts of Guwahati; Press Information Bureau, Bagurumba Dwhou cultural programme, 2026; Akashvani, Parikrama, Bodo musical traditions; Government of Meghalaya, About Meghalaya; District East Garo Hills, Festivals; District Aizawl, Dance; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Miscellaneous Arts and Crafts of Mizoram; District South Tripura, Culture; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Lok Sabha Starred Question 107, 11 December 2023, Annexure II. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Cheraw, the bamboo dance of Mizoram.

title: Folk and Tribal Dances of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura

body:
Arunachal Pradesh

Arunachal Pradesh has numerous tribal dance traditions associated with agricultural cycles, religious ceremonies, social celebrations and oral narratives.

DanceCommunityFestival or association
PonungAdiSolung and community celebrations
PopirGaloMopin festival
Aji LamuMonpaTraditional dance-drama
DelongAdiEtor festival
YakjongAdiAran festival

Ponung is traditionally performed by Adi women, particularly during Solung, an important agricultural festival. Its songs may recount community traditions and beliefs.

Popir is closely associated with the Galo community and Mopin, a festival celebrating prosperity and agricultural well-being.

Rekham Pada is another important traditional dance associated with Arunachal Pradesh.

Nagaland

The dances of Nagaland reflect the distinct cultural identities of its numerous Naga communities. Traditional performances are connected with agricultural festivals, community feasts, celebrations and historical martial traditions.

Chang Lo is commonly associated with the Chang community. Zeliang dance traditions include group performances connected with seasonal celebrations and social occasions.

The Hornbill Festival provides a common platform for the presentation of dances and other cultural traditions belonging to different communities. It should not be confused with a particular tribal dance.

CommunityAssociated festival
AngamiSekrenyi
AoMoatsu
KonyakAoleang
ZeliangMileinyi

These festivals provide important settings for traditional songs, dancing and community participation. Drum accompaniment, collective singing and distinctive costumes are prominent in many Naga performances.

Manipur

Thabal Chongba

Thabal Chongba is a traditional group dance associated with the Yaoshang festival, celebrated around the time of Holi. Participants commonly join hands and dance collectively.

Lai Haraoba

Lai Haraoba is a traditional religious festival of the Meitei community. Its ritual dances, music and ceremonies are associated with the worship of traditional deities and narratives concerning creation and community life.

Pung Cholom and Sankirtana

Pung Cholom is a drum dance associated with the devotional traditions of Manipur. The pung, a traditional drum, is both a musical instrument and a central feature of the performance.

Manipuri Sankirtana is a broader Vaishnava devotional tradition combining singing, drumming and dancing. It expresses devotion to Krishna and is performed during religious festivals and ceremonies connected with important stages of life.

In 2013, UNESCO inscribed Sankirtana, ritual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipur on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Manipuri is one of India's classical dance forms. Thabal Chongba, Lai Haraoba ritual dances and Sankirtana belong to related but distinct cultural and religious traditions of Manipur.

Sikkim

The Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali communities have contributed distinctive dance traditions to Sikkim.

DanceCommunityIdentifying feature
Singhi ChhamBhutiaSnow lion dance
Yak ChhamBhutiaYak costume and mountain pastoral life
MaruniNepaliFestive and social dance
Tamang SeloTamang communityDamphu drum
Chu-FaatLepchaWorship associated with Mount Khangchendzonga
Zo-Mal-LokLepchaSowing, reaping and harvesting of paddy

Singhi Chham, also written as Singyee Chaam, represents the snow lion and is associated with auspicious celebrations, including Pang Lhabsol.

Monastic Cham dances are Buddhist ritual performances involving masks, ceremonial costumes, horns, cymbals and drums. Related traditions also exist in Ladakh and other Himalayan regions.

Prelims focus

  • Ponung: Adi community and Solung.
  • Popir: Galo community and Mopin.
  • Thabal Chongba: Manipur and Yaoshang.
  • Pung Cholom: Manipur and the pung drum.
  • Singhi Chham: Sikkim and the snow lion.
  • Trap: Aji Lamu belongs to the Monpa tradition of Arunachal Pradesh, not the Mizo tradition.

[References: District East Siang, Government of Arunachal Pradesh, Culture and Heritage; Sangeet Natak Akademi, National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Lok Sabha Starred Question 107, 11 December 2023, Annexure II; Nagaland State Portal, People and Culture; Nagaland Department of Information and Public Relations, Hornbill Festival cultural performance reports; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India; UNESCO, Sankirtana of Manipur, nomination file 00843 and Decision 8.COM 8.14; Sikkim Tourism, Music and Dance; Tribal Research Institute and Training Centre, Government of Sikkim, Bhutia Tribe. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

body:
The role of musical accompaniment

Music provides rhythm, melody and emotional expression in Indian folk and tribal dances. Traditional instruments are frequently made from locally available materials such as wood, bamboo, animal hide, gourds and metals.

Some dances are closely identified with a particular musical instrument. Others use clapping, songs or rhythmic striking of objects to accompany movement.

Classification of musical instruments

Traditional Indian musical instruments can be classified according to the source of the sound they produce.

CategorySound productionExamples
Avanaddha VadyaVibration of a stretched membraneDhol, dholak, pung, dhamsa, chenda
Ghana VadyaVibration of a solid objectManjira, cymbals, chimta, khartal
Sushira VadyaVibration of airPepa, poongi, flute, shehnai, nadaswaram
Tata VadyaVibration of stringsTumbi, ektara, ravanhatta, serja

Drums such as the dhol belong to the membrane instrument category. Manjiras consist of metal discs that produce sound when struck together and therefore belong to the solid percussion category.

Pepa and poongi are both wind instruments, but they are associated with different cultural traditions. Pepa is traditionally made using a buffalo horn and is associated with Assamese Bihu. Poongi is closely associated with the snake-charming heritage of the Kalbelia community.

Important dance-instrument pairs

DanceState or regionCharacteristic accompaniment
GarbaGujaratDhol and manjira
Terah TaliRajasthanManjiras
KalbeliaRajasthanPoongi and khanjari
BhangraPunjabDhol and tumbi
LavaniMaharashtraDholki
ChhauEastern IndiaDhamsa, dhol and mohuri
BihuAssamDhol, pepa, gogona and toka
BagurumbaAssamKham, siphung and serja
Dollu KunithaKarnatakaDollu drum
KaragattamTamil NaduNadaswaram and tavil
Pung CholomManipurPung drum
Tamang SeloSikkimDamphu
GhumuraOdishaGhumura drum

These instruments are characteristic associations rather than exclusive pairings. The dhol, for example, is widely used in several states and cannot be assigned to only one dance.

Distinguishing musical instruments from performance props

Traditional dances frequently incorporate objects that help identify a performance. Such objects may produce rhythm, represent an occupation, symbolise religious beliefs or contribute to the visual identity of the dance.

  • Dandiya Raas uses wooden sticks that also produce rhythmic sounds.
  • Gof Gunthan uses ropes to form intertwined patterns.
  • Tippani uses a traditional floor-compacting implement.
  • Karagattam and Rajasthani Bhavai involve balancing vessels.
  • Kachchhi Ghodi uses a dummy horse costume.
  • Cheraw uses bamboo poles that also produce rhythmic accompaniment.

Prelims focus

  • Pepa: buffalo-horn wind instrument associated with Bihu.
  • Poongi: wind instrument associated with Kalbelia.
  • Manjira: metallic percussion instrument associated with Terah Tali.
  • Dholki: characteristic accompaniment of Lavani.
  • Pung: traditional drum of Manipur.
  • Trap: Manjira is a solid percussion instrument, whereas dhol is a membrane percussion instrument.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 10: Theatre Crafts, pp. 117-121; UNESCO, Chhau Dance and Kalbelia Folk Songs and Dances of Rajasthan; Incredible India, Bihu Dance; Karnataka Tourism, Dollu Kunitha; Sikkim Tourism, Music and Dance; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]
